title: Bowing to elders across the line
hook: Arjuna sees his elders across the field, and why Hindus touch elders' feet.
carry: bow to your elders, even across the line
tomorrow: what happens to Arjuna's body when he sees them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Gita's first chapter, Arjuna asked to be set in the middle, and we kept: god chose to drive arjuna's chariot. Krishna stops it, and speaks one line.

At a family gathering, there's a moment at the door: before shoes come off, before the hellos, many Hindu kids bend down to touch a grandparent's feet. Arjuna gets his doorway moment on a battlefield. Krishna stops the chariot in front of Bhishma, the grandsire who helped raise him, and Drona, his teacher, and says one line: partha pashyaitan samavetan kurun iti. Partha, look at these Kurus gathered here. What Arjuna sees isn't an army anymore. It's the people he would bow to.
screen: `A BOW AT THE DOOR.` → `PARTHA, LOOK.` → `NOT AN ARMY: HIS ELDERS.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya gives the list: tatrapashyat sthitan parthah pitrn atha pitamahan, acharyan matulan bhratrn putran pautran sakhims tatha. There Partha saw them standing: fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends. Every word is someone you'd bow to, or someone who'd bow to you. And that bow is the teaching. The Mahabharata tells what happened just before the fighting began. Arjuna's eldest brother, Yudhishthira, took off his armor, laid down his weapons, and walked on foot across the field toward the enemy line. Both armies thought he was giving up. He wasn't. He went to Bhishma, to Drona, to Kripa, another teacher, and to his uncle Shalya, bowed at their feet, and asked for their blessing and their leave to fight. And each of them blessed him. That's how deep this runs in Hindu life. Many families greet an elder by bending to touch their feet, a pranam, and the elder lays a hand on the head and blesses: live long, be well. It isn't about who's right. It honors what an elder has given, and asks for what they can still give. Arjuna sees his elders on the other side of a war, and the tradition still says: they're your elders. Today that might mean the relative you've argued with. In a Hindu home, you still bend down when you walk in.
screen: `FATHERS, TEACHERS, UNCLES, FRIENDS.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA WALKS ACROSS, UNARMED.` · `HE BOWS AND ASKS A BLESSING.` · `PRANAM: A BOW, A BLESSING.` · then, large: `ELDERS STAY ELDERS.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus begin a visit, a puja, even an exam day, by bowing to an elder. If an elder is near, greet them today with folded hands or a bow. If not, bring one to mind, maybe even one you've disagreed with, join your palms, and bow your head a little toward them. If you don't pray, simply hold their face in mind with gratitude. Then rest with the breath until the sit is done.
Pranam: the bow to an elder, often to their feet. Yudhishthira gave it across a battle line, and his elders blessed him.
Keep this one: bow to your elders, even across the line. Yudhishthira did, on foot. See you at the next verse.

fork.setup: you walk into a family gathering, and the uncle you argued with is in the good chair by the door. what does Yudhishthira's walk across the field suggest?

fork.reveal: Yudhishthira walked across a battlefield to bow to Bhishma and Drona and ask their blessing. elders stay elders, even across the line.

original.note: Sanskrit: samavetan, gathered together: Krishna's word for the Kurus he tells Arjuna to look at, kin on both sides.
